extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English literature / literary history
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical observations about composing short, periodical essays in the style of the early-18th-century Tatler/Spectator: tone, aims, subject choice, frequency, and methods for using wit and satire to influence a broad reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit directed to a useful end
rubrics_metrics.description: "wit, if a man had it, unless it be directed to some useful end, is but a wanton, frivolous quality; all that one should value himself upon in this kind is that he had some honourable intention in it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist's wit should serve an honourable purpose (moral instruction, public good, reform of follies) rather than mere cleverness for its own sake. Steele and Addison used wit to encourage virtue and check frivolity; imitators who used wit only for ornament failed to have the same effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cheerful, unpretending influence (restraint of earnestness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep deep earnestness restrained within the bounds of a cheerful, unpretending influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serious intentions should be delivered with a light touch—gentle, kind humour that avoids heavy-handed moralizing so the message is persuasive without alienating readers. Steele deliberately avoided pedantry and blunt moralizing in favour of a modest voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appealing to passions or pedantry of moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not appeal to passions or affect pedantry of moralizing; avoid heavy-handed exhortation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most effective essays persuade by reasoned wit and example rather than by inflaming passions or preaching. Steele 'would affect no pedantry of moralizing, he would appeal to no passions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use familiar ways and common incidents (everyday accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place everyday life and common incidents before the reader as seen by a natural and honest man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exquisite grace and kindliness tied to familiar incidents make learning amiable and widely appealing (tea-tables, coffee-houses, merchants), helping literature reach readers who previously avoided such topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence and regular publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence is built 'drop by drop' via regular, frequent publication (e.g., thrice-weekly Tatlers, daily Spectators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularity (daily or several-times-weekly issues) habituates readers and spreads influence; small, consistent contributions can have cumulative moral and cultural effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial entertainments over mere garnish
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize substantial content rather than surface garnish or fashionable trappings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitators who copied only the superficial 'garnish' of the papers (titles, characters like 'Night Cap') but lacked substantial entertainments and insight were unsuccessful; the real value lies in substantial, thoughtful pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requires fine, particular manner of thinking and exact knowledge of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: This style demands a particular intellectual temperament and an exact knowledge of the world which makes it hard to imitate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful essayists possess a blend of judgment, experience, and subtle observation; clubs of lesser wits found themselves unable to match the original manner despite attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censure actions/things not persons (avoid personal scandal)
rubrics_metrics.description: When exposing vice, aim at actions and public things rather than attacking persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defoe's 'Scandal Club' declared 'The Business of this Society is to censure the Actions of Men, not of Parties... They do not design to expose Persons but things.' Tactful censure preserves moral authority and avoids alienation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use allegory and gentle satire to expose follies
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ allegory and light satire to reveal societal follies (e.g., the allegory of Modesty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allegory and whimsical stories entertain while making pointed observations; such devices allow critique without rancor and can amaze readers into self-recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance wit and learning without pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine wit, nice judgment, and learning so that learning is amiable and not pedantic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Spectator succeeded by pairing learning with grace and humour, making literature accessible to merchants and ladies alike; excessive learnedness or pedantry weakens popular appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstain from personality in political argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in political debate with 'unexampled abstinence from personality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele's political pamphleteering aimed to argue principles rather than attack individuals; avoiding personal attacks preserves respectability and broad support even when taking strong stands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use authoritative or news material sparingly to lend weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally use news or office-derived information to give weight and acceptance to writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steele thought it permissible to use news obtained via office to support his writing because it brought weight to arguments; such material should be used judiciously to bolster credibility without dominating the essay's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose and vary subjects judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects must be well chosen and varied judiciously to maintain interest and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of Addison's later volume notes that some subjects were 'not always well chosen or varied judiciously' which weakened the work; careful editorial selection and variety sustain readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make literature amiable and attractive to broad social classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Dress learning so it becomes a 'welcome guest at tea-tables and assemblies' and is relished by merchants and ladies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aim is to rescue learning from pedants and present it attractively across social strata; tone, subject matter, and clarity should all support broad accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate format and length for public consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Short, readable formats (penny papers, occasional half-sheets for post, short diversions at end of papers) suit the public's appetite for 'a little reading at a time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pieces to match readers' attention spans (brief essays, small diversions at the end of a paper); format choices (price, frequency, possibility to send by post) aided dissemination and readership.
